Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-13 Introduction: April 10, 2025 Faculty Senate Meeting Amends the Faculty Senate By-Laws to Restructure The Center Review Subcommittee RATIONALE: The Faculty Senate Executive Committee, in conjunction with the existing Center Review Subcommittee, and representatives from the Office of the Provost, have been working all year to update the University’s definitions and classification system for all center and institute (C/I) types.
This comprehensive update initiative has clarified and expanded requirements around budgeting, reporting, application and renewal for all C/I’s.
This major change is expected to increase the workload of the Center Review Subcommittee and the working group agreed that the subcommittee should thus become a full, permanent standing committee as part of this shift.
A By-laws amendment to Section 4 of Appendix C is therefore proposed.
According to Section 12.1 of the By-Laws, amendments require two meetings and a two-thirds majority vote of senators present to pass.

University of Rhode Island Faculty Senate INITIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON TECHNOLOGY AND INFRASTRUCTURE

The CTI’s Goals and Objectives for AY 23-24: Overall Goal: Continue collaboration with Information Technology Services and review and make policy recommendations regarding the implications on academic and research planning, standards, services, physical facilities, and allocation of resources on all matters pertaining to information technology, infrastructure, computing, communications, and networking. Primary objectives for AY 23-24: • Ensure protection of academic freedom in all matters related to IT. • Advocate for all faculty’s teaching and research needs to be met in all matters related to IT.

Challenges and Issues the CTI hopes to address during AY 23-24: • URI Secure wifi difficulties from Linux (affecting students and faculty) • Proofpoint blocking emails from AAUP (faculty union); gets into larger issue of academic freedom and URL rewriting (the latter affects the readability of URLs in recipient’s inboxes, which presents issues for instruction) • eCampus replacement (tentatively Workday for the HR, financial, and administrative components, particularly the need for demos, faculty input); we don't want a repeat of Brightspace • Although we may have no input into the Workday transition for HR, Financials, etc., we may have influence on the student module

Challenges and Issues the CTI hopes to address during AY 23-24 (continued): • Draft a letter to CIO about IT security mandates: specifically the user policy that may have conflicts with how University policies are enacted - may overlap with CBUM. At some institutions, one can opt out of the standard configuration. At others, this is not an option: • How does this affect academic freedom? • Letter would need to strike the right balance • National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has the draft of a cybersecurity policy available ( NSPM 33) and, if implemented, may affect University faculty and students. Apparently, this has not been shared with the faculty. Understanding how it will be implemented and affect research is essential.

Challenges and Issues the CTI hopes to address during AY 23-24 (continued): • How does ITS’s budget allow them to handle unforeseen expenditures that may arise mid-year, such as the need to respond to a critical systems vulnerability? • How does the university (e.g. facilities, police, etc.) handle both faculty and teaching staff (TAs) getting access to labs or classrooms as needed; at the same time, how are security concerns (such as being able to lock a classroom from the inside in the case of a lockdown) addressed?

Faculty Senate Executive Committee

Through RI General Law §16-32-10, academic responsibility at URI is delegated to the President and the Faculty Senate. The Faculty Senate Executive Committee (FSEC) serves as the steering committee of the Senate. It represents the Senate in meetings with other University bodies and with the Provost, the President, and the URI Board of Trustees. Meetings of the FSEC are held weekly to coordinate the Senate’s business and its committees and address concerns within its jurisdiction.
For the description of the powers and duties of the Executive Committee, please see University Manual Appendix C: By-laws of the Faculty Senate, Section 4.1 – 4.9.

COMMITTEE REVIEW PROCESS The committee were able to continue the practice established by the 2022-3 committee of seeking three reviews per proposal for the Career Enhancement proposals. However, due to the significant increase of proposals in Proposal Development and Collaborative Proposal

Development, the committee must reduce to two reviews per proposal for these two categories.
This year’s committee only has 4 members, much smaller than previous years (7 members in 2024-5 and 10 members in 2023-4).
For that reason, the committee relied on 6 other members of the Committee for Research and Creative Activities as well as 25 previous awardees to contribute reviews.
Each committee member (10 total) reviewed 5-6 proposals, and each external reviewer reviewed 2-3 proposals.
Proposals were assigned so that at least one committee member reviewed each proposal.
The committee attempted to assign knowledgeable reviewers to each proposal while avoiding conflicts of interest.
The nature of the competition, however, means that most proposals were reviewed by faculty outside their discipline.
The committee created rankings of the proposals in each funding category based on the reviewer scores and comments, but the committee discussed the merits of each proposal, focusing particularly on proposals with variable scores and on proposals close to the funding threshold.
In situations where ratings were very similar, the committee gave preference to junior faculty.

The committee created a written summary of the deliberation for each proposal in the Career Enhancement category and most proposals in the Collaborative Proposal Development category.
We acknowledge that reviewers are likely to differ in the range of scores assigned and checked the possibility that a reviewer might give consistently “high” or “low” scores respectively.
Because the number of proposals reviewed per reviewer is low, our ability to correct for reviewer “leniency” was limited.
RECOMMENDATIONS FOR 2027 Be prepared to handle more proposals The number of proposals increased substantially in both Proposal Development and Collaborative Proposal Development, while remaining relatively stable in Career Enhancement.
This growth has made it challenging for the subcommittee to manage the workload and secure enough qualified reviewers.
We anticipate that proposal volume will remain at this level or continue to rise next year.
To address this, we may need to (1) expand the size of the committee and (2) seek additional review support from colleagues who are not previous awardees.

Emphasize the expectations in more detail The RFP states that this is a campus-wide competition and that proposals will be reviewed by non-experts.
While most PIs appeared to understand and appreciate this, some submissions seemed to be revised versions of proposals originally prepared for specific agencies and therefore included a level of technical detail that may not be accessible to a generalist audience.
Regarding plans for future external submissions, reviewers expected applicants to identify not only a specific target agency or program but also a realistic timeline.
Several proposals did not include a timeline and were consequently scored lower.
Placing additional emphasis on this requirement in future RFPs would help applicants avoid unnecessary point deductions.

Communicate expectations from reviewers Reviewers may benefit from more explicit guidance on both the criteria and process for evaluating proposals. For example, using prior external funding as an example some reviewers assigned lower scores to applicants with extensive previous awards, while others scored them more favorably. Similarly, for the Career Enhancement category, some reviewers assumed that awards are primarily intended for assistant professors, which is not the case. Providing more detailed and standardized review criteria would help improve consistency across evaluations. REPORT OF THE PRESIDENT a.
Report: Responding to the question previously raised, President Parlange explained his generaldesire to free up faculty time for greater research endeavors.
He did not intend to give faculty theimpression that he was issuing a blanket statement regarding the discontinuation of lowenrollment courses.

He did, however, intend to issue a charge to the community that every courseand program deserves a fresh and honest look at its value.
The President offered a brief slide presentation that highlighted several recent events aroundcampus and the community.
He then addressed a Senate-approved bill from the Novembermeeting that he has opted not to sign.
The rationale was related to his foregoing comments as henoted that the university has long been and continues to be in something of a budgetarypredicament.
While the faculty control the curriculum, the financial metrics of the curriculum areultimately his responsibility.
Over time, he hopes to expand the community’s understanding of thebudget choices that are continuously being made and empower department heads and deans toundertake more robust budgetary assessments of curricular proposals before they reach theFaculty Senate.
In the case of the specific unsigned proposal, which called for a new track withinthe Mathematics Ph.D., the President’s understanding is that the program is not large and the newtracks appear to require the teaching of additional classes, the enrollments for which arereasonably expected to be very small.

It did not appear to the President that the proposal wasadequately vetted through a wider lens, considering existing similar or related programs.
Facultymembers from the Mathematics department disagreed, noting that the proposal had been indevelopment for three years and had been considered from all angles.
The department is awarethat the program is small and they considered the subject proposal a means of attracting morestudents.
Further, the new track may not actually involve additional instructional duties forfaculty.
It was speculated that the full details and rationale may not have come through in thewritten proposal, in which case the current setting is likely not the place to debate its merits.
Other questions, unrelated to the unsigned bill, were directed to the President.
One pertained tostaff-hiring trends at the University.
President Parlange’s budget presentation at the Novembermeeting had offered metrics on URI’s standing among peer institutions where addingtenure-track research faculty is concerned, but the university’s standing with regard to addingstaff members was not addressed.
No such numbers were available.

It was noted that the University has an admirable goal of attracting new international students asgraduate assistants, but not much has been said about the level of support such students requireand how the university will afford it.
Housing and English language instruction are importantconsiderations and without these services, this goal will be difficult to meet.
President Parlangestated he continues to advocate for funding support and to look for new ways to raise revenues 2

for these purposes.
A question was raised by Engineering faculty about the university’s burdensome systems andprocess requirements, especially where grant funding is concerned.
A multi-million dollaropportunity was recently lost due to problems with InfoEd, the University’s electronic researchadministration system.
President Parlange stated he would look into this issue. b.

OLD BUSINESS: Continuation of tabled discussion (from the 10/20/22 meeting) regarding Senatemeeting venue/modality going forward.
A motion was made and seconded to “return to the regularorder of in-person Senate meetings with in-person voting, beginning in January, with meetingswebcast for community viewing.” The motion was debated at length with various individuals statingtheir preference for either a full return to in-person meetings or a continuation of the hybrid meetingoption.
Most comments seemed to favor allowing the hybrid option to remain.
The Parliamentarianadvised that the motion may not be eligible for a vote as it had implications for the Senate By-Laws.Senate By-Laws amendments require two readings.
The Senate President ruled that the motion was inorder, as a By-laws amendment was not explicitly proposed.
A roll-call vote was called for andconducted.
The motion to return to a strictly in-person modality failed (13 aye; 36 nay) and FSPresident Rice announced that the hybrid modality would continue to be available next semester. 8.
